title: JSON.stringify, parse, and structured clone
hook: JSON is the wire format of the web — but it is not a full copy of JavaScript values. `JSON.parse` can execute attacks if you trust the wrong input, and `JSON.stringify` silently drops `undefined`, functions, and `Symbol` keys.

blocks.text: **JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)** is a text format for structured data. **`JSON.stringify(value)`** converts a JavaScript value to a JSON string. **`JSON.parse(text)`** converts JSON text back to JavaScript values. JSON supports only `null`, booleans, numbers, strings, arrays, and objects — not `undefined`, functions, `Symbol`, `bigint` (without custom handling), `Date`, `Map`, or `Set`. **`structuredClone()`** (modern browsers and Node 17+) deep-clones most structured data including `Date`, `Map`, and `ArrayBuffer` — but still cannot clone functions or DOM nodes.

entries.plainDefinition: Serializes a value to JSON text. Omits undefined properties, converts NaN/Infinity to null in arrays, throws on BigInt.
Parses JSON text into JavaScript values. Returns plain objects and arrays — no type information. Security risk with untrusted input.
Optional callback that transforms each key-value during parse — use for Date revival or validation.
Deep clone using the structured clone algorithm. Handles cycles, Dates, Maps — not functions or symbols.

blocks.text: Every REST API and localStorage call uses JSON. Assuming `JSON.parse` returns typed data causes production bugs — `id` arrives as number or string depending on the server. `JSON.stringify` dropping `undefined` means `{ status: undefined }` becomes `{}` silently. Security: never pass untrusted JSON to `eval` or template engines. Prototype pollution attacks use `__proto__` keys in parsed objects. C# `System.Text.Json` deserializes to typed classes; JavaScript `JSON.parse` always returns plain objects unless you validate and map.

blocks.title: Security first
blocks.body: Treat all external JSON as hostile. Use `JSON.parse` (not `eval`). Validate shape after parse. Reject `__proto__` and `constructor.prototype` keys. Consider `Object.create(null)` for dictionaries. For deep merge, use libraries that block prototype pollution.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Choose the right tool
items.body: Wire format / storage → JSON. Deep clone in memory → `structuredClone`. Custom types → write mapper functions.

items.title: stringify with awareness
items.body: Know what drops: `undefined`, functions, symbols. `Date` becomes ISO string. `toJSON()` on objects customizes output.

items.title: parse then validate
items.body: Never trust parsed shape. Check types with typeof, Array.isArray, or schema library (Zod).

items.title: Handle BigInt and Date
items.body: BigInt: convert to string before stringify. Date: revive in reviver or map manually after parse.

snippet.explanation: Lines 2–3: eval on JSON is RCE. Lines 6–14: __proto__ merge pollutes Object.prototype. Lines 17–22: reject dangerous keys. Line 25: null-prototype objects prevent inherited pollution.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `eval` to parse JSON. Assuming parsed dates are Date objects. Expecting `undefined` properties to survive stringify. Not validating API responses. Deep merging parsed JSON into existing objects without prototype pollution guards. Using JSON.parse + stringify as a deep clone — loses types and breaks on cycles.

blocks.text: JSON.parse is safe from code execution (unlike eval) but not safe from data attacks. Prototype pollution (CVE-class in lodash.merge, hoek, and others) exploits __proto__ keys. Use Map for untrusted key-value data or Object.create(null). JSON.parse reviver runs bottom-up on nested values. JSON.stringify replacer can filter keys. toJSON() on objects customizes serialization (Date uses this). For API design: document whether numbers are integers or floats; JavaScript loses precision above 2⁵³. C# System.Text.Json can deserialize to record types with validation attributes — JS needs Zod/Yup/io-ts. structuredClone uses the HTML structured clone algorithm — supports transferable objects in workers. JSON.parse('null') returns null; JSON.parse('') throws.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Recommending eval for JSON. Not knowing stringify drops undefined. Saying JSON.parse returns typed objects. Ignoring prototype pollution when merging parsed JSON. Not mentioning BigInt stringify throws.

interviewTakeaways: JSON supports null, boolean, number, string, array, object — nothing else natively.
JSON.stringify drops undefined properties; JSON.parse returns plain objects.
Never use eval for JSON — use JSON.parse; still validate shape after parse.
Prototype pollution: reject __proto__ and constructor keys; use Object.create(null).
60s: JSON wire format only. Parse then validate. No eval. structuredClone for deep copy. BigInt needs string.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'JSON.parse is safe.' Strong: 'No code execution but prototype pollution and missing validation are real risks.'
Using JSON round-trip as deep clone — loses Date type, fails on cycles.
Strong answer: 'Parse, validate schema, reject __proto__. structuredClone in memory. BigInt as string.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS JsonValue/JsonObject types describe JSON-safe values. JSON.parse still returns any — use Zod or type guards at boundaries.
C# deserializes to typed records with validation. JS JSON.parse is untyped — you must map and validate manually.
